title: Human Spleen Anatomy: Red Pulp, White Pulp & Blood Flow

Protected beneath ribs nine through eleven in the upper left abdomen, the spleen is the largest lymphoid organ in the body and a precision filter for circulating blood. Known in classical anatomical nomenclature as Lien (splen), this chapter belongs to the lymphatic & immune study pathway. Blood enters the spleen through the splenic artery and percolates through two compartments. White pulp — cuffs of lymphocytes around central arterioles — mounts immune responses to blood-borne antigens, making IgM and opsonins. Red pulp is a mesh of sinusoids and cords where old, stiff or antibody-coated red cells are trapped and destroyed by macrophages, and where platelets are stored (a third of the body's pool). In fetal life the spleen makes red cells; after splenectomy the liver and marrow take over, but the loss of opsonisation leaves lifelong risk of encapsulated bacterial sepsis.

When you trace how human spleen anatomy functions in the living body, each documented landmark contributes a specific mechanical or physiological step. Key structures covered in this guide include Capsule & trabeculae (structural framework and conduit for vessels), Red pulp (filters senescent and abnormal red cells; recycles iron; stores platelets and monocytes), White pulp (immune surveillance of blood: antibody and opsonin production, especially against capsules), and Splenic sinusoids (the mechanical filter: healthy deformable cells pass; rigid ones are eaten). By following all 20 illustrated landmarks in sequence, you can see how gross morphology, internal chambers or layers, and surrounding vessels work as one integrated unit.

Understanding these structural relationships is essential for both anatomy exams and real-world physiological reasoning. Practical anatomical correlations also stand out: for capsule & trabeculae, the capsule is thin and the pulp fragile — the spleen tears easily in blunt abdominal trauma and bleeds briskly; for red pulp, in hereditary spherocytosis the rigid spheres are trapped here, causing haemolytic anaemia cured by splenectomy. questions.question: What is the spleen's function?
questions.answer: The spleen filters blood, removes aging red blood cells and helps immune cells respond to blood-borne material. Its red and white pulp perform different tasks. In relation to periarteriolar lymphoid sheath, this structure samples blood-borne antigens with nearby immune cells.

questions.question: Can you feel a normal spleen?
questions.answer: A normal adult spleen is usually protected beneath the left lower ribs and is not readily felt on examination; enlargement is a medical finding, not something this atlas can diagnose. In relation to splenic vein, this structure returns filtered blood to the portal system.

questions.question: What is the capsule & trabeculae?
questions.answer: A fibroelastic capsule sending trabeculae into the pulp, carrying the vessels. Function: Structural framework and conduit for vessels. In relation to capsule & trabeculae, this structure structural framework and conduit for vessels.

questions.question: Where is the white pulp located?
questions.answer: Periarteriolar lymphoid sheaths (T cells), follicles (B cells) and a marginal zone rich in macrophages. Function: Immune surveillance of blood: antibody and opsonin production, especially against capsules. In relation to white pulp, this structure immune surveillance of blood: antibody and opsonin production, especially against capsules.

questions.question: What is the function of the hilum?
questions.answer: Function: Vascular gateway; also the site of accessory spleens in ~15% of people. The notched medial border where splenic vessels enter and the tail of pancreas and stomach fundus relate. In relation to hilum, this structure vascular gateway; also the site of accessory spleens in ~15% of people.
